MCACN 2026: Chrysler 300 Display Brings Together All Letter Series Models (1955-1965)
19 photos
Photo: Jay Moser/YouTube
The 2026 Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals (MCACN) took place this weekend, bringing hundreds of classic muscle cars under the same roof. But this year's edition also included a very cool Chrysler 300 display. Reserved for "letter series" cars, it featured vehicles from each model year.
The "letter series" debuted in 1955 as the first Chrysler to sport the 300 emblem. It's called the "letter series" because each version had a different letter next to its 300 suffix. The series began with the C-300, but the cars built from 1956 to 1965 were named 300B to 300L. Chrysler skipped the letter I.
The original C-300 was in fact a homologation special. Essentially a full-size hardtop with a beefed-up engine, it was offered for public consumption so that Chrysler would be able to race it in NASCAR. The 1955 version featured a 331-cubic-inch (5.4-liter) FirePower V8 rated at 300 horsepower, hence the 300 name. Chrysler sold 1,725 units.
In 1956, Chrysler increased output to 340 horsepower but also offered a higher compression ratio variant of the engine good for 355 horsepower. The latter made the 300B the first American car to produce one horsepower per cubic inch. Design changes were minimal, and sales dropped to 1,102 examples.
Photo: Jay Moser/YouTube The 300C arrived in 1957 with a more flamboyant design. Additionally, the "letter series" gained a larger 392-cubic-inch (6.4-liter) Hemi good for 375 horsepower. Some 18 examples got a 390-horsepower version of the mill. The 300C was the first "letter series" model available as a convertible. Deliveries rose to 2,402 units.
Largely similar to the 300C, the 1958 300D was the last "letter series" to use the FirePower Hemi V8. It was now rated at 380 horsepower, with a fuel-injected version available (390 horsepower). The latter, however, was quickly discontinued due to reliability issues. The 300D moved only 809 examples.
The 300E arrived in 1959 with minor styling changes but with big news under the hood. The FirePower unit was dropped in favor of the 413-cubic-inch (6.8-liter) Golden Lion V8 . Rated at 380 horsepower, the 300E found 647 customers.
The Golden Lion remained in use in 1960, but output dropped slightly to 375 horsepower. However, Chrysler produced a 400-horsepower "short ram" version. The 300F had brand-new styling, but the large rear fins were still a thing. A four-speed manual was available for the first time. Sales recovered and reached 1,217 examples.
Photo: Jay Moser/YouTube The 1961 300G arrived with yet another redesign, which included slanted quad headlamps and smaller tailfins. Output remained unchanged at 375 horsepower, while the special-order four-speed manual was no longer available. The three-speed unit returned. Exactly 1,617 examples were delivered that year.
The 300H version of 1962 retained the previous year's front clip, but the rear fins were entirely gone. Still powered by the Golden Lion V8, the 300H came with 380 horsepower on tap. 1962 saw the introduction of the not-so-exclusive Chrysler 300 Sport . "Letter series" sales reached a new low, with only 570 units delivered.
For 1963, the 300J returned to quad horizontal headlamps while gaining a more angular trapezoidal grille. The Golden Lion was, again, Chrysler's choice for oomph, increasing output to 390 horsepower. The convertible version was no longer available for the first time since 1956. The four-speed manual became available. With only 400 units sold, the 300J is the rarest "letter series" car out there.
Chrysler made only minor adjustments to the design, but the 1964 300K arrived with a four-barrel version of the Golden Lion as standard. It was rated at 360 horsepower. The cross-ram version was now an option. The convertible returned, and Chrysler made the "letter series" a bit cheaper by removing some luxury items. Sales reached an all-time high at 3,647 examples.
Photo: Jay Moser/YouTube The final iteration of the "letter series," the 1965 300L , arrived with a brand-new styling with crisp lines and slab sides. The cross-ram unit was removed from the options list, with the four-barrel 413 Golden Lion remaining the sole powerplant. Output was 360 horsepower, as in the previous year. The 300L sold 2,845 units. Although Chrysler showed a clay model of the 1966 300M in late 1963, the car never went into production.
The MCACN display is obviously packed with nicely restored models, but it also includes a few cars we may never see somewhere else. The list includes the 1958 300D pilot car (the first ever built, also fitted with the fuel-injected engine) and the supercharged 1960 300F that reached nearly 180 mph (290 kph) at Daytona. An unrestored 1961 300G was also on display.
Hit the play button below to check them all out. And when you do, tell me which one you liked the most in the comments section below. I'm a big fan of the first-year C-300, but I also love the 1957 300C and 1961 300G. The finless 1962 300H also looks cool in the convertible layout.
